strengths: Novel graph prior design combining multiple SBMs and preferential attachment that thoughtfully addresses limitations of single SBM approaches
Solid experimental methodology with 10 runs, multiple datasets spanning diverse domains, and comprehensive baseline comparisons
Strong finetuning results on accessible datasets (7 of 10 show best performance, with substantial improvements on several datasets like artnet-exp and hm-prices)
Demonstrates importance of pretraining via Table 4 comparison with random graph adapters, validating the pretraining contribution
Honest and comprehensive limitations discussion, acknowledging scalability constraints, domain coverage gaps, and task restrictions
Reasonable architectural design choices that reduce computational overhead (e.g., initializing from pretrained LimiX, freezing backbone layers)
weaknesses: Severe scalability limitations prevent evaluation on 31% of datasets (4 of 13 fail with OOM during finetuning), undermining state-of-the-art claims where method cannot run on some benchmark datasets

Inconsistent and often weak in-context learning performance with substantial gaps on some datasets (hm-prices: -6.94%, city-roads-M: -5.6% vs G2T-LimiX), suggesting poor prior coverage of certain real-world graph types

Insufficient validation of graph prior quality—no quantitative comparison of structural properties (degree distributions, clustering, motifs) between synthetic and real graphs despite this being central to PFN framework

Limited experimental analysis with missing ablations on critical design choices (MGM loss weight=0.1, attribute mixing probability p, importance of each SBM component) and no analysis of learned attention patterns
Incomplete comparisons with concurrent work (TabGFM mentioned but not evaluated) and missing important baselines from related work
Modest novelty in core components—graph adapters are straightforward message-passing extensions; main contribution is graph prior design which is incremental over existing techniques

strengths: First successful implementation of PFN framework for graphs, demonstrating the viability of extending tabular foundation models with graph-aware components
Strong finetuning results on diverse datasets (7/10 where feasible), with improvements of 2+ percentage points on several tasks (artnet-exp, hm-prices, artnet-views)
Clean architectural design with interpretable three-level attention hierarchy; sparse message-passing adapters well-motivated and technically sound
Comprehensive evaluation across 13 datasets with diverse properties (homophilous/heterophilous, varying densities, multiple domains and task types)
Thoughtful graph prior combining stochastic block models with preferential attachment to generate realistic community and core-periphery structure
Honest and detailed limitations discussion; clear ablation (Table 4) demonstrating importance of pretraining for finetuning performance
Reproducible experimental setup with 10 runs, mean/std reporting, and clear train/validation/test splits
weaknesses: In-context learning performance substantially underperforms the core claim: GraphPFN (ICL) consistently trails G2T-LimiX (ICL) by 5-10 percentage points on most datasets, contradicting the 'foundation model' narrative that depends on strong ICL capabilities

Prior mismatch limits generalization: fails on dense graphs (hm-prices: 10.7M edges vs 194K max in prior, ~11pp gap) and domain-specific graphs (traffic networks like city-roads-M, ~5.6pp gap), suggesting the prior underspecifies real-world graph diversity

Severe scalability issues: OOM failures preventing finetuning on 3/13 datasets; limited to ≤50K nodes and ≤10 classes; requires 8 A100 GPUs for 6 days of pretraining, limiting practical applicability and reproducibility

Limited technical novelty: sparse attention adapters are standard, SBM+BA+SCM prior combines existing techniques with minimal innovation, and approach is primarily engineering-focused rather than methodologically novel

Insufficient ablations due to computational constraints: no ablation on MGM loss weight (0.1) or strategy, no comparison of freezing vs. fine-tuning LimiX layers, no ablation on prior components, no investigation of why ICL fails on specific datasets

Unclear attribution of finetuning gains: Table 4 doesn't cleanly separate the contribution of (a) powerful message-passing adapters vs. (b) pretraining itself; random adapter baseline conflates architectural advantage with pretraining benefit

Weak prior validation: synthetic graphs lack quantitative comparison with real-world statistics (degree distribution, clustering coefficient, assortativity); visualizations appealing but insufficient for validating PFN framework assumptions

Reproducibility concerns: no code release despite claiming 'first publicly available' implementation; unjustified hyperparameter choices (e.g., why p=0.1 for edge sampling in MGM loss?); massive computational barrier to reproduction
Unexplained pattern in LapPE results: sometimes helps ICL, sometimes hurts it (e.g., facebook: 91.45 vs 90.23), suggesting incomplete understanding of the method

Limited analysis of learned patterns: no visualization of representations, no analysis of what graph dependencies the model captures, no investigation of failure modes on heterophilous graphs (questions dataset shows 12.30 vs 15.31 for baseline)

strengths: Novel and principled graph prior design combining multiple SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCMs for realistic synthetic graph generation
Strong finetuning results achieving state-of-the-art on 7/10 tested datasets with improvements >2 percentage points on several benchmarks
Elegant architecture that leverages pretrained LimiX features while adding trainable message-passing adapters, maintaining per-feature token structure
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse datasets with multiple modalities, task types, and homophily properties
Honest and detailed discussion of limitations in Appendix A, including scalability, prior mismatch, and scope restrictions
Solid technical contribution validated by ablation study (Table 4) demonstrating importance of pretraining
Clear presentation with effective architectural diagrams and synthetic graph visualizations
First successful implementation of PFN framework for graph data (to authors' knowledge)
weaknesses: Critical scalability limitations: tested only on ≤50K nodes with out-of-memory errors on finetuning for 3/13 datasets; entire-graph-in-memory requirement fundamentally incompatible with modern large-scale graphs and undermines 'foundation model' claims

Poor generalization to out-of-distribution graph types directly contradicts foundation model motivation: significantly worse ICL on large-scale graphs (hm-prices) and domain-specific structures (traffic networks in city-roads-M)

Mixed in-context learning performance: ICL often inferior to finetuned baselines, and substantially worse than G2T-LimiX on multiple datasets, suggesting synthetic pretraining fails to capture transferable ICL patterns—core PFN theoretical advantage is lost

Limited ablations acknowledged by authors: no analysis of MGM loss contribution, SBM vs BA importance, design choices (frozen LimiX, hyperparameter selections), or message-passing architecture variants
Significant experimental scope restrictions: ≤10 class classification only, node-level tasks only, requires PCA for high-dimensional features, no link prediction or graph classification capability
Lack of interpretability analysis: no visualization of learned patterns, error analysis, or investigation of whether model performs genuine in-context learning versus memorization

Design choices lack principled justification: why scaled dot-product attention over GNN variants? Why freeze LimiX? Why MGM weight 0.1? Theoretical implications of mixed supervised+MGM loss on posterior approximation unclear
Incomplete comparison: limited comparison with other pretrained graph models beyond G2T-FM; no ablations to understand which components drive performance gains

strengths: First PFN-based model genuinely pretrained on synthetic graph data with graph-aware objectives (supervised + masked graph modeling), advancing beyond hand-crafted feature approaches like G2T-FM and TAG
Thoughtfully designed graph prior combining multi-level SBMs, preferential attachment, and graph-aware SCMs; well-validated in Appendix B with numerical analysis and ablations on simpler alternatives
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 13 diverse datasets, 10 runs with std, both ICL and finetuning settings, multiple baseline comparisons, and good ablations (e.g., Table 5-6, Figure 2)
Strong empirical results: achieves best performance on 10/13 datasets when finetuned with ensembling, often by substantial margins (≥1 percentage point on multiple datasets)
Honest discussion of limitations in Appendix A (scalability, prior domain coverage, class restrictions, task scope) and clear reproducibility (training details, code promised, ablations provided)
Clear presentation with helpful figures (especially Figure 1 architecture diagram) and comprehensive appendix with graph characteristic analysis and visualization
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: graph adapters are standard scaled dot-product attention masked by adjacency matrix. Main novelty resides in the graph prior design, not the architecture itself

Restricted experimental scope: limited to small-medium graphs (largest ~170K nodes) and ≤10 classes; excludes >10 class problems due to TFM limitations. This significantly constrains claims about practical utility on modern graph benchmarks

Ad-hoc design choices with insufficient justification: MGM loss weight (0.1) not ablated; freezing LimiX layers except adapters not compared to unfrozen alternatives; GNN neuron mixing probability discretization and multi-level SBM construction both appear unmotivated

Statistical significance concerns: Many ICL improvements are small (1-2 percentage points, often within error bars). Ensembling provides large gains, but makes single-model comparisons harder to interpret. Some baseline results missing (TAG on GraphLand datasets)

Incremental contribution over prior work: primary differences from G2T-FM are adding message-passing adapters and using graph prior instead of hand-crafted features. While useful, this represents contained advancement rather than fundamental innovation

Scalability not addressed: acknowledged limitation that entire dataset must be processed at once leads to significant memory consumption. No exploration of sampling-based or memory-efficient alternatives discussed

Incomplete ablation studies: missing comparisons on supervised vs. MGM loss weighting; unclear how much improvement comes from pretraining vs. architecture vs. ensembling; random adapter ablation (Table 6) helps but is limited in scope

Graph prior coverage concerns: synthetic statistics show high variance in some dimensions (e.g., average degree 2.39-479 vs. real 3.75-460), and prior is acknowledged to not cover specific domains like traffic networks

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation with 13 diverse datasets across multiple baselines, including recent graph foundation models (G2T-FM, TAG)
Novel graph prior combining multi-level stochastic block models with preferential attachment thoughtfully designed to capture both community and core-periphery structure observed in real graphs
Strong empirical results achieving state-of-the-art on 10/13 datasets after fine-tuning with consistent improvements across different dataset types
Honest treatment of limitations in Appendix A, transparently discussing scalability issues, domain bias, and task restrictions
Validation that pretraining is critical (Table 6 shows substantial performance drops with random adapters), supporting the importance of the graph prior
Well-written paper with clear motivation, good figures, and detailed experimental protocols including multiple runs with standard deviations
Thorough graph prior analysis (Appendix B.2) demonstrating alignment of synthetic graph characteristics with real-world datasets
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: graph adapters are only 1-hop sparse attention, a straightforward extension with no justification for why this simple approach suffices compared to multi-layer message passing used in standard GNNs

Incremental technical contribution: primarily combines existing components (LimiX foundation model, sparse attention, graph generation); the main insight—pretraining on synthetic graphs helps—is somewhat expected

Frozen backbone during pretraining constrains learning: only graph adapters are updated while all LimiX layers remain frozen; no ablation justifying this restriction or exploring full model fine-tuning

Graph prior design appears ad-hoc: multi-level SBM bijection mapping lacks principled justification; Table 5 shows simpler baselines (Erdős–Rényi, single SBM) perform comparably on several datasets, undermining claims about prior importance

Modest empirical improvements: many gains are only 1-2 percentage points (e.g., city-reviews 80.49→80.14, hm-prices 79.26→76.27) without formal significance testing; unfair comparison to non-pretrained G2T-FM and TAG rather than fairly-pretrained baselines

Critical scalability limitations severely restrict practical applicability: requires entire dataset in memory, acknowledged by authors as major constraint; small datasets (max ~168k nodes) prevent evaluation on realistic large graphs

Restricted scope significantly limits impact: limited to node-level tasks only (no link prediction, graph classification), ≤10 classes (inherited from LimiX), excludes datasets larger than medium scale
Lack of mechanistic insight: no visualization or analysis of what graph adapters learn, when/why message passing helps, or how in-context learning works with only 1-hop attention

Confounding experimental factors: 8 random features added per forward pass mentioned only in footnote; unclear how much performance gain comes from this regularization vs. graph pretraining; some datasets require PCA preprocessing (amazon-ratings) while others don't without clear justification

Missing ablations on architectural choices: no study of message-passing depth, attention mechanism alternatives, or why 1-hop is sufficient; only Table 6 validates pretraining importance, not adapter design
Experimental design concerns: pubmed evaluation only in ICL setting because model ran out of memory during fine-tuning, suggesting memory efficiency issues even on modest-scale datasets

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear presentation of why graph foundation models are challenging and how PFNs address this
Novel graph prior combining multi-level SBMs with preferential attachment; Appendix B.2 provides good empirical validation of structural alignment with real graphs
Solid experimental evaluation: comprehensive baselines, 10 runs with variance, both ICL and finetuning settings, proper ablations (Tables 5-6) demonstrating importance of prior and pretraining
Consistent empirical improvements across 13 diverse datasets (10/13 wins when finetuned); honest limitations discussion in Appendix A
Good reproducibility: code availability, detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Core architectural contribution is incremental: adding sparse attention layers to LimiX is fairly straightforward; main novelty concentrated in graph prior design
Modest empirical gains in ICL setting where foundation models should excel: GraphPFN (ICL) average rank 5.67 vs. G2T-LimiX 7.33 on GraphLand, with many datasets showing <1% improvement
Severe scalability limitations acknowledged but not addressed: requires full dataset in memory, restricting to small/medium datasets (≤168K nodes); solutions mentioned (TabICL, sampling) not explored

Narrow scope undermines foundation model claim: node-level tasks only, ≤10 classes inherited from LimiX, no link prediction or graph-level tasks; 13 datasets is limited for foundation model evaluation

Graph prior is domain-specific (social/information networks): acknowledged mismatch on city-roads-M (Table 5) where simpler Erdős-Rényi works better; extending to traffic/geometric graphs left as future work
Key design choices lack justification: 1-hop vs. multi-hop attention (no ablation), adding 8 random features, MGM loss weight (0.1), freezing LimiX layers—no ablation studies for these
Missing computational analysis: no inference time comparisons with baselines; pretraining cost (7 days on 8 A100s) not contextualized against alternatives
Bidirectional message passing between test nodes in ICL setting not justified or ablated—potential information leakage between test samples not discussed
Graph prior has many hyperparameters; limited sensitivity analysis beyond Table 5 makes adaptation to new domains challenging
